dialogue:
[pharmacist] Hello, I see you’re here to pick up your new prescription. Are you Mr. Julian Thorne?
[patient] Yes, that’s me. I’m a bit tired, I just got back from a trip to Kyoto last week.
[pharmacist] I’m sorry to hear you’re feeling exhausted. This is Amoxicillin, an antibiotic to treat the respiratory infection Dr. Sarah Vance diagnosed.
[patient] Right, Dr. Vance at St. Luke’s Medical Center in Chicago referred me to you for the counseling.
[pharmacist] She’s a good doctor. Just to confirm, you have a history of mild hypertension, correct?
[patient] Yes, I’ve been managing that for a few years now.
[pharmacist] This antibiotic is generally safe for hypertension, but you should still take it with food to avoid stomach upset.
[patient] Got it. How often do I need to take this?
[pharmacist] One tablet, twice a day, for seven days.
[patient] I started feeling sick about five days ago, right after I returned from Japan.
[pharmacist] That timing makes sense. The infection likely set in while you were traveling.
[patient] I had a chest X-ray on October 12th that was clear, but I got worse after the trip.
[pharmacist] We know. The CT scan Dr. Vance ordered yesterday showed signs of community-acquired pneumonia.
[patient] It’s annoying. I have a huge work project due next week.
[pharmacist] Rest is crucial. Do you have any family helping you out?
[patient] My brother, Leo, is 32 and staying with me, and my daughter, Mia, is 8, but she’s with her mom.
[pharmacist] It’s good to have support. Make sure Mia doesn’t have any contact with you while you’re contagious.
[patient] I’m aware. I’ll wear a mask when I’m around her.
[pharmacist] Good idea. Do you have any questions about the side effects?
[patient] Can it interact with my blood pressure medication?
[pharmacist] No, Amoxicillin does not interact significantly with standard antihypertensives like Amlodipine.
[patient] That’s a relief. I was worried.
[pharmacist] Just stay hydrated. If you develop a rash or difficulty breathing, stop the medication and call 911.
[patient] Understood. I’ll call Dr. Vance if I don’t improve in two days.
[pharmacist] That is the right plan. Your insurance, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois, covers this fully.
[patient] Great. The number is 4482-9910-2231 if you need to verify.
[pharmacist] I have it on file. Is there anything else I can help you with?
[patient] No, I think that’s everything. Thanks for your help.
[pharmacist] You’re welcome. Get well soon, Mr. Thorne.

dataset: robust-an operative report: pre- and post-opera
dialogue:
[pharmacist] Good morning, Mrs. Kowalska. Please, have a seat. I see you have a new prescription for apixaban from Dr. Weber at the St. Agnes Clinic.
[patient] Good morning. Yes, Dr. Weber said I need to start this because of the blood clot risk after my knee surgery.
[pharmacist] Exactly. This medication is an anticoagulant, which means it thins your blood to prevent clots. It is very important for your recovery.
[patient] I am a little nervous. My daughter, Ewa, is 34, and she worries constantly about my health. She is calling me every day.
[pharmacist] That is very sweet of her. Is Ewa living with you, or is she visiting?
[patient] She lives in Berlin, but she is here this week to help me. She is very protective.
[pharmacist] I understand. Now, let's discuss how to take the medication. You will take two tablets, 5 milligrams each, twice a day.
[patient] Twice a day? With meals or without?
[pharmacist] It does not matter if you take it with food or on an empty stomach, but consistency is key. I recommend taking it with your morning and evening meals so you don't forget.
[patient] I usually have breakfast at 7 AM and dinner at 7 PM. That sounds manageable.
[pharmacist] Perfect. What is the best place for you to keep the medication?
[patient] I am staying at my sister's house for now. Her name is Marta. She is 75 and lives at Lindenweg 4, 12345 Posen.
[pharmacist] Noted. I will send the prescription details to that address if you wish, or you can pick it up here.
[patient] I will pick it up here, but I will store it at Marta's house. She has a good routine.
[pharmacist] That is fine. Just make sure Marta knows the importance of not missing a dose.
[patient] I will explain it to her carefully. She is very reliable.
[pharmacist] One important point: do not take any other blood thinners or aspirin unless Dr. Weber specifically tells you to.
[patient] I used to take aspirin for my head, but I stopped a few months ago.
[pharmacist] Good. Also, watch out for signs of bleeding, such as blood in your urine or stool, or unusual bruising.
[patient] What if I cut myself while cooking? I am not very steady on my feet yet.
[pharmacist] Minor cuts may take a little longer to stop bleeding. Use pressure and a bandage. If it doesn't stop in 10 minutes, call us.
[patient] I will be careful. My nephew, Jan, is 28, and he is helping with the housework, so I won't be cooking much.
[pharmacist] That is good to have help. How is your mobility? Are you using a walker?
[patient] Yes, I have a rollator. I can walk a bit, but my knee is still swollen.
[pharmacist] That is normal for the first few weeks. The medication helps prevent clots in the deep veins of your legs, which is a risk after knee surgery.
[patient] I see. So this is to save my leg?
[pharmacist] It is to prevent a pulmonary embolism, which is a clot traveling to the lungs. That is a serious condition we want to avoid.
[patient] I did not know that. Thank you for explaining it.
[pharmacist] You are welcome. Do you have any other medications?
[patient] I take metformin for diabetes and lisinopril for blood pressure.
[pharmacist] Those are safe to take with apixaban. Just keep taking them as prescribed by your general practitioner.
[patient] My GP is Dr. Schneider. He referred me to the clinic for the surgery.
[pharmacist] I see Dr. Weber's notes. He coordinated with Dr. Schneider. That is good practice.
[patient] Yes, they work well together. Dr. Schneider checks my blood sugar weekly.
[pharmacist] Excellent. Is there anything else you would like to ask before we finish?
[patient] No, I think I understand. I will tell Marta and Ewa about the schedule.
[pharmacist] Great. I will print out a pill organizer chart for you.
[patient] That would be very helpful. Thank you, Ms. Fischer.
[pharmacist] You are welcome, Mrs. Kowalska. Take care, and call us if you have any concerns.

OPERATIVE REPORT

PATIENT NAME: Kowalska, Barbara
DATE OF BIRTH: 14-03-1952
MRN: 882345-01
DATE OF OPERATION: 24-05-2024
SURGEON: Dr. Heinrich Weber
ASSISTANTS: Dr. Lukas Brandt, RN Sofia Miller
ANESTHESIA: Spinal anesthesia with local infiltration
ANESTHESIOLOGIST: Dr. Clara Voss

PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Osteoarthritis of the right knee (ICD-10-CM M17.12)
POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Osteoarthritis of the right knee; Total knee arthroplasty site

PROCEDURE:
Total knee arthroplasty, right knee, posterior-stabilized system.

FINDINGS:
1. Advanced tricompartmental degenerative joint disease of the right knee with significant cartilage loss and subchondral sclerosis.
2. Moderate varus deformity of the limb axis.
3. No evidence of infection or fracture.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A midline longitudinal incision was made over the anterior aspect of the right knee. The extensor mechanism was split in the midline. The patella was everted laterally. The anterior, medial, and lateral parapatellar soft tissues were released as needed to allow full extension and flexion.

The distal femur was resected using a cutting guide to achieve a 90-degree distal femoral angle. The posterior condyles were resected to match the implant size. The proximal tibia was resected perpendicular to the mechanical axis of the tibia. The tibial tunnel for the post was drilled.

A 54 mm posterior-stabilized femoral component was cemented in place. A 54 mm tibial component with a 54 mm insert was cemented into the tibia. The patella was resurfaced with a 12 mm patellar button. The extensor mechanism was closed in two layers with absorbable sutures. The skin was closed with subcuticular sutures and skin staples.

The wound was inspected and was dry. A sterile dressing was applied. The limb was splinted in full extension. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the PACU in stable condition.

[nurse] good afternoon , this is sarah from st. jude’s icu . i’m calling to check on mr . arthur penhaligon who was discharged this morning . is he there ?
[patient] yes , hello . it’s arthur . i’m sitting on the sofa , feeling a bit tired but mostly okay .
[nurse] that’s good to hear , arthur . how is your breathing compared to when you were in the hospital ?
[patient] it’s better , but i still feel a bit wheezy if i move around too much . i tried to get up to the bathroom and my chest felt tight .
[nurse] i see . have you taken your medications as prescribed ? specifically the nebulizers and the blood pressure pills ?
[patient] yes , i took the nebulizer at 08:00 and the tablets with my breakfast . i haven’t eaten much , just some toast .
[nurse] did you have any fever or chills since coming home ?
[patient] no fever . maybe a little shiver this morning , but i think it was just the cold from the window .
[nurse] okay . let’s check your pulse . do you have a monitor or do you want me to guide you through a manual check ?
[patient] i have the blood pressure cuff they gave me . it’s on the side table .
[nurse] great . can you put the cuff on your left arm and start the machine ?
[patient] okay , starting it now . one moment .
[nurse] take your time .
[patient] it’s done . it says 135 over 88 .
[nurse] that’s slightly elevated but acceptable given your history . how is your heart rate ?
[patient] the machine didn’t show heart rate , just blood pressure . i can count my pulse if you like .
[nurse] please do . place two fingers on the inside of your wrist and count for 15 seconds .
[patient] okay.. . one , two , three.. .
[nurse] tell me the number when you finish 15 seconds .
[patient] it was 28 beats .
[nurse] so that’s 112 per minute . that’s a bit fast . are you feeling anxious or in pain ?
[patient] not anxious . i’m just worried about this tightness . i don’t want to go back to the hospital . i have my rugby club match on saturday .
[nurse] i understand , arthur . the heart rate is likely due to the residual infection or the pain from the chest tightness . let’s try another nebulizer treatment . do you have the salbutamol inhaler with you ?
[patient] yes , it’s on the coffee table .
[nurse] please take two puffs , wait 30 seconds , and take two more . then let me know how you feel .
[patient] okay , doing that now .
[nurse] i’ll stay on the line .
[patient] .. .
[patient] that’s done . i feel a bit looser in the chest , but still a bit puffy .
[nurse] that’s a positive response . the tightness seems to be related to bronchospasm rather than a cardiac event , especially since the blood pressure is stable .
[patient] good . i was really worried . i’ve been managing the accounts at henderson & co for forty years , i don’t want to stop now .
[nurse] you’re doing well . since your heart rate is elevated , i’m going to increase your follow-up . i’d like you to come to the clinic tomorrow at 10:00 am for a chest x-ray and bloods .
[patient] tomorrow ? that’s soon . can i wait until wednesday ?
[nurse] given the heart rate of 112 , i’m not comfortable waiting three days . we need to rule out any progression of the pneumonia .
[patient] fine . 10:00 am . i’ll need to drive there . is the clinic open ?
[nurse] yes , it’s on the main floor . please bring your insurance card . your provider is careplus health .
[patient] i have it here . the number is cp-4492-11 .
[nurse] noted . also , please monitor your temperature every four hours . if it goes above 38.0 degrees , or if you feel chest pain that radiates to your jaw , call 999 immediately .
[patient] 38.0 , got it . and the email ? you said i should send you the readings .
[nurse] yes , send them to s.miller@stjudes-nhs.uk . subject line should be arthur penhaligon daily report .
[nurse] do you have any questions before we hang up ?
[patient] no , i think that’s clear . just trying to get back to normal life .
[nurse] rest as much as possible , arthur . avoid lifting heavy things for at least a week .
[patient] understood . thanks , sarah .
[nurse] goodbye , arthur . take care .

dialogue:
[nurse] Good morning, this is Sarah from the St. Jude Medical Center surgical triage line. May I have your name and date of birth?
[patient] Yes, hello. My name is Arthur P. Vance. I was born on May 12, 1941.
[nurse] Thank you, Mr. Vance. Can I have your medical record number, please?
[patient] It should be on my card. Let me look. It is MJ-49201-B.
[nurse] Thank you. What seems to be the problem today?
[patient] My right knee is really swollen and it hurts when I try to walk. It started about three days ago.
[nurse] I see. Did you fall or have any specific injury to the knee?
[patient] No, no fall. I was just gardening in my yard in Cleveland, and it just got worse over the last few days.
[nurse] Okay. Is there any redness or heat around the knee?
[patient] It looks a bit red, yes, and it feels warm to the touch.
[nurse] Do you have a fever or chills?
[patient] I felt a little feverish last night, maybe around 101 degrees.
[nurse] I am concerned about a possible infection in the joint. Do you have a primary care physician or a doctor who referred you recently?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Elena Rostova at the Midwest Orthopedic Group. She saw me last week for some general aches.
[nurse] Did she recommend any specific treatment?
[patient] She said to take ice and anti-inflammatories, but it is not getting better.
[nurse] Where did you live before moving to Cleveland?
[patient] I lived in Duluth, Minnesota, for forty years before we moved here in 2015.
[nurse] I see. Did you work in Minnesota?
[patient] Yes, I worked for the Superior Foundry Company as a shift supervisor until I retired in 2006.
[nurse] That sounds like hard work. Do you have any family members who can help you if you need to come in today?
[patient] My son, David, is here. He is 54. My daughter, Sarah, is 50, but she is in Ohio.
[nurse] Thank you. Is David with you now?
[patient] Yes, he is in the other room.
[nurse] Do you have any allergies to medications, particularly antibiotics?
[patient] No, no known allergies.
[nurse] Are you taking any blood thinners?
[patient] I take aspirin 81mg every day, but that is it.
[nurse] Okay. Given your age and the symptoms, I need you to come in for an urgent evaluation. We need to check for septic arthritis.
[patient] That sounds serious. Is it?
[nurse] It can be, but we can treat it effectively if we catch it early. You need to come in now, not wait for a regular appointment.
[patient] I am a member of the Cleveland Model Railroading Club. I usually go there on Tuesdays, but I can skip it.
[nurse] Yes, please skip it. We need to prioritize your health. Can your son drive you?
[patient] Yes, David can drive me.
[nurse] Please go to the Emergency Department at the main entrance on 5th Avenue. Tell them you are here for an urgent surgical triage.
[patient] Okay, I will tell them my name and the referral from Dr. Rostova.
[nurse] Perfect. Do not eat or drink anything until we see you, in case we need to do a procedure.
[patient] Understood. Thank you, Sarah.
[nurse] You are welcome, Mr. Vance. Please go now.
[patient] Goodbye.
[nurse] Goodbye.

OPERATIVE REPORT

PATIENT: VANCE, ARTHUR P.
MRN: MJ-49201-B
DOB: 05/12/1941
AGE: 83
SEX: M
SURGEON: DR. JAMES H. THORNE, MD
ASSISTANT: DR. LENA K. MOSS, MD
ANESTHESIA: LOCAL ANESTHESIA WITH SEDATION
ANESTHESIOLOGIST: DR. R. GUTIERREZ
DATE OF PROCEDURE: 10/24/2023
PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: RIGHT KNEE JOINT PAIN, POSSITIVE SEPTIC ARTHRITIS
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: RIGHT KNEE SEPTIC ARTHRITIS, STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS
PROCEDURE: RIGHT KNEE ARTHROSCOPIC IRRIGATION AND DEBRIDEMENT

FINDINGS:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. Local anesthetic was infiltrated into the right knee joint. Under arthroscopic visualization, the joint space was found to be distended with turbid, yellowish fluid. The synovial lining was markedly erythematous and hypertrophic. No gross effusion was present in the suprapatellar pouch, but the joint capsule was tense. The articular cartilage of the femur and tibia showed moderate degenerative changes consistent with the patient's age. No meniscal tears or ligamentous instability were identified. The fluid was sent for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity. The joint was irrigated with 3 liters of normal saline and 2 liters of povidone-iodine solution. The joint was then lavaged with additional normal saline until the return was clear. The arthroscope and instruments were removed, and the incisions were closed with absorbable sutures. A sterile dressing was applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was placed in the supine position. After induction of sedation and local anesthesia, the right knee was marked. Two standard portals were established: anterolateral and anteromedial. The arthroscope was inserted through the anterolateral portal. The joint was inspected, confirming the findings described above. Lavage and debridement were performed as described. The total fluid volume used for irrigation was approximately 6 liters. Hemostasis was achieved. The procedure lasted approximately 45 minutes. The patient was transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) in stable condition.

DISPOSITION:
The patient is admitted for intravenous antibiotic therapy. Weight-bearing status is non-weight-bearing on the right lower extremity. Physical therapy to be initiated upon discharge.

DR. JAMES H. THORNE, MD

POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: OSTEOARTHRITIS, RIGHT KNEE
PROCEDURE: TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY, RIGHT

FINDINGS:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. The right knee was identified. A medial parapatellar approach was utilized. The extensor mechanism was retracted laterally. The joint capsule was incised and opened. There was significant synovial inflammation and osteophyte formation. The femoral and tibial condyles showed advanced cartilage loss consistent with severe osteoarthritis. No ligamentous laxity was noted beyond what is expected for the grade of arthritis. The patella showed chondromalacia grade III.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
Standard tourniquet was applied to the thigh and inflated to 250 mmHg. The medial and lateral parapatellar retinacula were released. The distal femur was resected using a computer-assisted navigation system to ensure correct alignment. The proximal tibia was resected perpendicular to the mechanical axis. The patella was resurfaced with a standard button. Trial components were inserted to assess stability, range of motion, and soft tissue balance. The knee was stable with no varus or valgus instability. Final components were cemented in place using polymethylmethacrylate. The extensor mechanism was closed with non-absorbable sutures. The subcutaneous tissue was closed with absorbable sutures. The skin was closed with staples and steri-strips. A sterile dressing was applied. The tourniquet was deflated. Hemostasis was confirmed. No active bleeding was noted. The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was 400 ml. No complications occurred.

DEAR DR. HADDAD,

I am writing to provide an update on the physiotherapy progress of Mr. Thilak Perera, who was referred to our practice following an acute injury to his left shoulder sustained on 12 Oct 2023 while working at Fournil Bleu.

HISTORY
Mr. Perera presented with acute onset of severe pain and weakness in the left shoulder after lifting a heavy crate. He reported a "pop" sensation followed by an inability to elevate the arm. Previous medical history includes a minor supraspinatus tear treated conservatively on 12 Oct 2021.

ASSESSMENT
Upon initial evaluation, Mr. Perera reported pain levels of 7/10 at rest and 9/10 with active movement.
- Range of Motion (ROM):
  - Abduction: 80 degrees (limited by pain)
  - Flexion: 90 degrees
  - External Rotation: 30 degrees
- Strength (MRC Scale):
  - Abduction: 3/5
  - External Rotation: 2/5
- Signs of inflammation were present, with mild swelling and warmth over the greater tuberosity.

TREATMENT PLAN
1. Acute Phase Management:
   - Cryotherapy for 15 minutes post-exercise.
   - TENS therapy for pain modulation.
   - Gentle pendulum exercises to maintain joint mobility without stressing the torn fibers.
2. Isometric Strengthening:
   - Introduction of isometric contractions for the rotator cuff muscles within a pain-free range.
3. Ergonomic Advice:
   - Discussed workplace modifications with Mr. Perera regarding his role at Fournil Bleu to prevent re-injury during the healing process.

PROGRESS
After three sessions of physiotherapy, Mr. Perera reports a reduction in pain to 4/10 at rest. He has demonstrated improved compliance with home exercises. There is a slight increase in active abduction to 90 degrees, though passive ROM remains limited. No adverse reactions to treatment have been observed.

PLAN

Elena Voss, MPT

ASSISTANTS: Dr. Lena Fischer, RN Sarah Okafor

PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Acute Cholecystitis
POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Acute Cholecystitis with Pericholecystic Fluid

PROCEDURE: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy

FINDINGS:
The abdomen was inspected laparoscopically. The gallbladder was found to be distended, erythematous, and edematous, consistent with acute inflammation. A moderate amount of pericholecystic fluid was present. The cystic artery and cystic duct were identified. There was no evidence of common bile duct stones. The liver parenchyma appeared normal.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
After establishing pneumoperitoneum and placing ports, the gallbladder was dissected from the liver bed using the critical view of safety. The cystic duct was clipped and divided. The cystic artery was coagulated and divided. The gallbladder was carefully dissected free from the gallbladder fossa. The gallbladder was placed in an extraction bag and removed through the umbilical port. Hemostasis was checked and found to be adequate. The ports were removed under direct visualization. No drains were placed.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was minimal. The patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the recovery area.

DISCHARGE PLANS:
The patient will remain admitted for observation. The next follow-up appointment with Dr. Hilem Gebremedhin at Kantonsspital St. Gallen is scheduled for 12 days post-operation at 14:30.

PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: ACUTE APPENDICITIS
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: ACUTE APPENDICITIS

PROCEDURE: LAPAROSCOPIC APPENDECTOMY

INDICATIONS: The patient is a 44-year-old male presenting with right lower quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. History of present illness suggests acute appendicitis. Ultrasound by Dr. Bianchi at Policlinico di Milano was inconclusive. CT abdomen/pelvis performed at our facility revealed an enlarged, inflamed appendix with periappendiceal fluid.

FINDINGS:
1. Incisions: Three 10-12 mm incisions were made at the umbilicus, left lower quadrant, and right lower quadrant.
2. Exploration: No evidence of peritonitis. Free fluid noted in the pelvis. The appendix was found to be distended, erythematous, and edematous, measuring approximately 3 cm in diameter. The tip was gangrenous.
3. Procedure: The mesoappendix was divided using harmonic scalpel. The base of the appendix was ligated with a 6.0 mm endoloop. The appendix was amputated 1 cm from the cecum and placed in a retrieval bag. The cecal stump was inspected and no bleeding was noted.
4. Lavage: The peritoneal cavity was irrigated with 2 liters of warm saline.
5. Hemostasis: No active bleeding.
6. Specimen: The appendix was sent to pathology.

COURSE OF OPERATION: The patient tolerated the procedure well. Vital signs remained stable throughout. Estimated blood loss was less than 50 ml.

POSTOPERATIVE PLAN:
1. Admit to surgical ward.
2. IV fluids and pain management.
3. Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily (given penicillin allergy).
4. Diet: Clear liquids as tolerated.

PROCEDURE: ARTHROSCOPIC PARTIAL MENISCECTOMY, LEFT KNEE

FINDINGS:
1. LATERAL COMPARTMENT: Normal cartilage. No loose bodies.
2. MEDIAL COMPARTMENT: A bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus was identified. The tear extended from the posterior horn to the mid-body. The free edge was unstable and causing mechanical symptoms.
3. ANTERIOR COMPARTMENT: Normal patellar cartilage. ACL and MCL intact.
4. POSTERIOR COMPARTMENT: PCL intact. No signs of synovitis.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was placed in the supine position after pre-operative antibiotics were administered. The left leg was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A tourniquet was applied to the upper thigh and inflated to 250 mmHg. Standard arthroscopic portals were established at the anterolateral and anteromedial locations. A 30-degree arthroscope was introduced into the joint. Diagnostic arthroscopy of all four compartments was performed as detailed in the findings.

The unstable bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus was reduced. Assessment of the tear revealed that the tissue was degenerative and not amenable to repair. Therefore, a partial meniscectomy was performed. Arthroscopic shavers were used to resect the unstable free edge of the meniscus, preserving as much healthy tissue as possible. The resected tissue was removed. The joint was irrigated with normal saline. Hemostasis was achieved. The arthroscope and instruments were removed. The portals were closed with simple interrupted sutures. Sterile dressings and a compression wrap were applied. The tourniquet was deflated. No intraoperative complications occurred. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the post-anesthesia care unit in stable condition.

POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Acute Suppurative Appendicitis

FINDINGS:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard fashion. The abdomen was insufflated to 12 mmHg. Three ports were placed: one 10mm umbilical port, one 5mm left mid-clavicular line, and one 5mm suprapubic port. Upon entry, the appendix was identified in the right lower quadrant. The appendix was dissected free from the omentum and the cecum. A titanium clip was placed at the base of the appendix, followed by division of the appendiceal stalk. The abdomen was lavated with 3 liters of warm normal saline. The ports were removed under direct vision. The skin incisions were closed with subcuticular sutures. Sterile dressings were applied. SUBJECT: PROGRESS REPORT – RIGHT KNEE OSTEOARTHRITIS

CLINICAL HISTORY:
Ms. Rodriguez-Garcia is a 65-year-old female presenting with chronic right knee pain, diagnosed as osteoarthritis. She is seeking conservative management to maintain mobility ahead of a planned travel trip to Zurich. Her family history is notable for her mother’s history of total knee arthroplasty. She lives independently and is visited frequently by her daughter, Lucía (age 32), from Spain.

CURRENT STATUS:
Subjective:
The patient reports morning stiffness lasting approximately 60 minutes, which improves with movement. Pain is currently rated 4/10 on the NRS, localized to the anterior knee (patellofemoral region). Pain is exacerbated by stair descent. She has been adhering to ice therapy intermittently, reporting discomfort with the cold temperature, which may be contributing to residual inflammation.

Objective:
- Range of Motion: Right Knee Flexion 110 degrees, Extension -5 degrees (lag).
- Strength: Quadriceps 4/5 (MRC) on the right side; Hamstrings 4/5.
- Gait: Antalgic gait with cane use on the left side. Mild varus alignment noted.
- Palpation: Tenderness over the patellar tendon and medial joint line. No effusion.
- Special Tests: Positive patellar grind test; negative Lachman and McMurray.

ASSESSMENT:
The patient continues to exhibit signs of patellofemoral overload and medial compartment wear consistent with moderate osteoarthritis. The primary barriers to function are anterior knee pain and reduced quadriceps endurance. The intermittent use of ice therapy is likely perpetuating the morning stiffness. Given her upcoming trip to Zurich, which involves significant walking and uneven terrain, there is a risk of symptom flare-up if strength and neuromuscular control are not improved.

PLAN:
1. Continue with manual therapy to reduce anterior knee pain and improve patellar tracking.
2. Strengthening program: Focus on open-chain and closed-chain quadriceps exercises. Introduce isometric holds to reduce pain.
3. Patient education: Reinforce the importance of consistent ice application (15 mins, 3x/day) post-activity to manage inflammation. Discuss heat therapy for morning stiffness.
4. Functional training: Stair case practice with proper technique (good leg up, bad leg down).
5. Re-evaluate in 2 weeks. If pain remains >4/10 after 4 weeks, refer back for consideration of intra-articular injection.

SIGNED,

Licensed Physiotherapist

Date: 15 March 2024
From: Marco Rossi (Patient)
To: Dr. Elena Bianchi (Cardiologist)
Subject: Discharge Questions

Dear Dr. Bianchi,

I am writing to confirm my discharge from the hospital. I am feeling much better, but I have some questions regarding my medication and follow-up.

Firstly, could you please clarify the dosage of the new beta-blocker I was prescribed? I am currently taking metoprolol 50mg twice a day, but I am unsure if this is the correct long-term dose.

Secondly, I have noticed some mild dizziness when standing up quickly. Is this a common side effect, or should I be concerned?

Also, please confirm the date of my next appointment. I believe it is scheduled for two weeks from now, but I want to be sure.

Thank you for your care.

Sincerely,
Marco Rossi
Via del Lago 12
6850 Mendrisio
Tel: +41 91 123 4567
Email: marco.rossi56@swissmail.ch
Medical Record No: 8842-1956-RO

---
Date: 15 March 2024
From: Dr. Elena Bianchi (Cardiologist)
To: Marco Rossi (Patient)
Subject: Re: Discharge Questions

Dear Mr. Rossi,

Thank you for your message. I am glad to hear you are feeling better.

Regarding your metoprolol, the current dose of 50mg twice a day is appropriate for now. We will adjust it if necessary based on your heart rate and blood pressure at your follow-up.

The dizziness you are experiencing is a common side effect, especially when changing positions quickly. Please stand up slowly. If it persists or worsens, please contact us immediately.

Your next appointment is confirmed for 29 March 2024 at 10:00 AM. Please bring all your medication bottles with you.

Best regards,
Dr. Elena Bianchi
Cardiology Department
Swiss Medical Center

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Rossi. I am Dr. Moreau, the attending physician here.
[interpreter] Buongiorno, signor Rossi. Io sono la dottoressa Moreau, la medico curante qui.
[patient] Good morning, doctor. I am a bit confused about why I am here.
[interpreter] Buongiorno, dottoressa. Sono un po' confuso sul perché sono qui.
[doctor] You were brought in by ambulance after a severe allergic reaction. Do you remember what happened?
[interpreter] È stato portato in ambulanza dopo una grave reazione allergica. Ricorda cosa è successo?
[patient] Yes, I was eating lunch in Milan and suddenly my throat started to close up.
[interpreter] Sì, stavo pranzando a Milano e all'improvviso la gola ha iniziato a chiudersi.
[doctor] Did you take any medication before the meal?
[interpreter] Ha preso qualche medicinale prima del pasto?
[patient] I took my usual asthma inhaler, but I also had a new supplement from a health store.
[interpreter] Ho preso il mio normale inalatore per l'asma, ma ho anche avuto un nuovo integratore da un negozio di salute.
[doctor] What was the name of the supplement?
[interpreter] Qual era il nome dell'integratore?
[patient] It was called "Herbal Lung Clear". I bought it online.
[interpreter] Si chiamava "Herbal Lung Clear". L'ho comprato online.
[doctor] Do you have the box or the bottle with you?
[interpreter] Ha la scatola o la bottiglia con sé?
[patient] No, I left it at my apartment in Como. I live in Como.
[interpreter] No, l'ho lasciato nel mio appartamento a Como. Vivo a Como.
[doctor] Okay. Let's check your medical history. Who is your primary care physician?
[interpreter] Va bene. Controlliamo la sua storia clinica. Chi è il suo medico di base?
[patient] My doctor is Dr. Elena Vieri. She has a practice in Como.
[interpreter] Il mio medico è la dottoressa Elena Vieri. Ha uno studio a Como.
[doctor] And who referred you to our hospital in Turin?
[interpreter] E chi l'ha indirizzato al nostro ospedale a Torino?
[patient] The emergency team called Dr. Luca Bianchi at the University Hospital in Turin.
[interpreter] Il team di emergenza ha chiamato il dottor Luca Bianchi all'Ospedale Universitario di Torino.
[doctor] I see. Now, about your insurance. Can you provide your health insurer details?
[interpreter] Capisco. Ora, riguardo alla sua assicurazione. Può fornire i dettagli del suo assicuratore sanitario?
[patient] I am insured by AXA Health. My insurance number is AX-998210.
[interpreter] Sono assicurato con AXA Health. Il mio numero di assicurazione è AX-998210.
[doctor] Thank you. We will send the bills to them. Do you have any other allergies?
[interpreter] Grazie. Invieremo le fatture a loro. Ha altre allergie?
[patient] I am allergic to penicillin. I have been for a long time.
[interpreter] Sono allergico alla penicillina. Lo sono da molto tempo.
[doctor] Understood. Are you currently taking any other daily medications?
[interpreter] Compreso. Sta prendendo altri farmaci quotidiani?
[patient] I take Albuterol 200mcg inhaler twice a day.
[interpreter] Prendo l'inalatore di Albuterol 200mcg due volte al giorno.
[doctor] And do you take any over-the-counter painkillers?
[interpreter] E prende qualche analgesico da banco?
[patient] Sometimes Ibuprofen 400mg if I have a headache.
[interpreter] A volte Ibuprofen 400mg se ho mal di testa.
[doctor] Did you take the Ibuprofen today?
[interpreter] Ha preso l'Ibuprofen oggi?
[patient] No, I have not taken it since yesterday evening.
[interpreter] No, non l'ho preso dalla sera di ieri.
[doctor] Good. We need to be careful with aspirin and NSAIDs given your asthma.
[interpreter] Bene. Dobbiamo fare attenzione con l'aspirina e gli FANS dato il suo asma.
[patient] My friend Marco suggested I stop taking the supplement.
[interpreter] Il mio amico Marco mi ha suggerito di smettere di prendere l'integratore.
[doctor] That was a good suggestion. We will verify the ingredients.
[interpreter] È stata una buona suggerimento. Verificheremo gli ingredienti.
[patient] I just want to go home soon. I have work in Milan.
[interpreter] Voglio solo tornare a casa presto. Ho lavoro a Milano.
[doctor] You will be monitored for 24 hours. We will keep you safe.
[interpreter] Sarà monitorato per 24 ore. La terremo al sicuro.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I feel better now.
[interpreter] Grazie, dottoressa. Mi sento meglio ora.
[doctor] You are welcome. Rest now. We will see you in the morning.
[interpreter] Prego. Riposi ora. La vedremo domani mattina.

[nurse] Good morning, signora Rossi. I am Nurse Elena, taking over from Marco. How are you feeling this morning?
[patient] I am okay, but my left knee is very stiff. I can hardly bend it.
[nurse] I see. Let me check your chart. You were admitted yesterday for severe knee pain, correct?
[patient] Yes. It started last week after I came back from my trip to Rome.
[nurse] Rome can be rough on the joints with all the walking. Did you have any swelling before you arrived here?
[patient] A little, but it got much worse when I tried to climb the stairs at my apartment in Como.
[nurse] Your insurance is with Sanitas, correct? We need to process the pre-authorization for the CT scan.
[patient] Yes, my number is 889-4421-09. My daughter, Lucia, usually handles these things, but she is at work.
[nurse] No problem. I have your email, ros.anna.milano1948@example.com, where we can send the report once it is ready.
[patient] Thank you. By the way, my friend Marco, who lives next door, says I should stop my evening walks at the park.
[nurse] Doctor Bianchi mentioned that rest is important right now. He is concerned about a possible fracture or severe degeneration.
[patient] I used to play tennis with the club in Bergamo, but I stopped two years ago because of this pain.
[nurse] I remember seeing that in your history. You had an MRI in March 2023, and an X-ray in January 2023, right?
[patient] Yes, those were done at the hospital in Milan. They said it was just osteoarthritis, but it is getting worse.
[nurse] The new CT scan will give us a much clearer picture of the bone structure and any cysts.
[patient] I am nervous. I do not want to need another operation.
[nurse] We are just looking for the cause of the acute pain. The technician will come to get you in twenty minutes.
[patient] Can I call my neighbor, Marco, to let him know I am not coming for dinner?
[nurse] Of course. Is there anything else you need before we leave?
[patient] Just water, please. And maybe a blanket. I feel a bit cold.
[nurse] I will bring both. Try to keep your leg straight and avoid putting weight on it.
[patient] I will do my best. I really hope the scan shows nothing serious.
[nurse] We will know soon. I will stay with you until the technician arrives.

note:
PATHOLOGY REPORT

Patient Name: Maria Silva
Medical Record Number: MR-2099-4471
Age: 85
Date of Birth: 12 Feb 1939
Referring Physician: Dr. Aldo Vermeulen
Date of Specimen Receipt: 03 Nov 2023
Specimen Type: Gallbladder (laparoscopic cholecystectomy)

CLINICAL HISTORY
85-year-old female with history of recurrent right upper quadrant pain. Previous attempt at cholecystectomy on 14 May 2021 was aborted due to severe inflammation. Recent ultrasound on 12 Oct 2022 indicated biliary sludge. Patient presented with acute cholecystitis and signs of sepsis.

MACROSCOPY
The submitted specimen is the gallbladder, measuring 8.0 x 4.5 x 2.0 cm. The serosal surface is congested and covered with fibrinous exudate. The wall is diffusely thickened, measuring up to 1.2 cm, with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. The lumen contains 30 mL of purulent bile and multiple small, hard, brown stones ranging from 0.3 to 0.8 cm in diameter. No mass lesion is identified.

MICROSCOPY
Sections show acute and chronic cholecystitis. The mucosa is severely inflamed with ulceration, neutrophilic infiltration, and necrosis of the epithelium. The muscularis propria is thickened and edematous with extensive inflammatory cell infiltration, including lymphocytes and plasma cells. There is evidence of transmural inflammation extending into the perimuscular connective tissue. No dysplasia or carcinoma is identified. The inflammatory infiltrate is non-specific.

DIAGNOSES
1. Gallbladder, laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Acute suppurative cholecystitis with chronic cholecystitis.
2. Gallstones (cholelithiasis).

PATHOLOGIST
Dr. Elena Costa
Board Certified Pathologist
Ospedale Santa Lucia Pathology Department
Contact: pathology@santalucia.it

OPERATIVE REPORT
PATIENT: Dubois, Elise
MRN: 49201
DATE OF BIRTH: 14/05/2005
SURGEON: Dr. K. Berger
ASSISTANTS: Dr. L. Fontaine, R. Meier
ANESTHESIA: General Endotracheal
PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Symptomatic Cholelithiasis
POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Symptomatic Cholelithiasis
PROCEDURE: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy

FINDINGS:
The gallbladder was distended and contained multiple small calculi. The gallbladder wall was thickened but not inflamed. No evidence of acute cholecystitis. The cystic duct and artery were identified and ligated. The common bile duct was not explored.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was placed in the supine position. General anesthesia was administered. The abdomen was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A 10mm umbilical port was placed under direct vision. Insufflation was performed at 15 mmHg. Two 5mm ports were placed in the right midclavicular line and the epigastric region. The gallbladder was dissected from the liver bed using harmonic scalpel. The cystic duct and cystic artery were clipped and divided. The gallbladder was placed in a retrieval bag and removed through the umbilical port. The port sites were closed with absorbable sutures. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the recovery room.

ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS: 20 ml
FLUIDS: 1500 ml crystalloid
URINE OUTPUT: 250 ml
COMPLICATIONS: None

SURGEON: K. Berger, MD
ASSISTANT: L. Fontaine, MD
ANESTHESIOLOGIST: Dr. S. Weiss

The patient, a 74-year-old female, presented to the emergency department on October 24, 2024, following a mechanical fall in her bathroom. The patient reports slipping on a wet surface. REASON FOR ADMISSION: Acute exacerbation of Bipolar I Disorder, Manic episode with psychotic features. Patient reports 3 days of sleep deprivation, psychomotor agitation, and command auditory hallucinations threatening harm to children.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 37-year-old Kosovar Albanian woman residing in Bern. She presented via telehealth triage reporting severe insomnia (0 hours sleep in 72 hours), racing thoughts, and intense agitation. Patient describes hearing voices telling her her children are unsafe and that she is an unfit mother. She left her home to avoid potential harm to her children, who are currently with her husband, Besnik. Patient denies intent to self-harm but admits to feeling "out of control." She reports that her current medication regimen (Lithium 900mg BID, Quetiapine 400mg QHS) is ineffective. She states she has been non-adherent to the morning dose of Quetiapine for the past 3 days due to feeling "too wired" to sleep, which paradoxically increased her agitation.

PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY
Diagnosis: Bipolar I Disorder.
Previous Hospitalizations: Last admission was 15/06/2021 to 29/06/2021 for a similar manic episode.
Outpatient Visits: Most recent outpatient visit was 14/10/2023.
Medical History: No significant medical history.
Substance Use: Denies alcohol or illicit drug use.

MEDICAL WORKUP
Lab results from 02/11/2023 showed normal Lithium levels (0.8 mEq/L) and normal TSH.
Toxicology screen performed in ED (14/02/2024 10:15): Negative for drugs of abuse.
Lithium level (14/02/2024 10:30): 0.6 mEq/L (subtherapeutic).

MENTAL STATUS EXAMINATION
Appearance: Well-groomed, female of stated age. Wearing casual clothing. Appears tense and disheveled hair.
Behavior: Psychomotor agitation. Pacing during interview. Poor eye contact. Fidgeting with hands.
Speech: Pressured, rapid, loud. Tangential but coherent.
Mood: "Anxious," "Explosive."
Affect: Labile, ranging from irritable to tearful. Congruent with stated mood.
Thought Process: Flight of ideas. Loose associations.
Thought Content: Auditory hallucinations (command type). Persecutory ideation regarding her husband's trust in her. No suicidal ideation. No homicidal ideation toward self or others, but significant fear of accidental harm to children due to lack of control.
Perception: Auditory hallucinations. No visual hallucations reported.
Cognition: Alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Concentration impaired due to agitation.
Insight: Fair. Patient recognizes she is ill and needs help.
Judgment: Impaired. Made decision to leave home abruptly to protect children, but is currently in an unsafe environment (public park).

ASSESSMENT
1. Bipolar I Disorder, Current Episode Manic with Psychotic Features
2. Insomnia, acute
3. Risk of harm to others (children) secondary to psychotic symptoms

PLAN
1. Admit to closed psychiatric unit for safety and stabilization.
2. Initiate IV Lorazepam 2mg for acute agitation.
3. Resume and titrate Lithium. Monitor levels q12h.
4. Continue Quetiapine 400mg QHS. Consider adding Risperidone if agitation persists.
5. Contact family (husband Besnik Hoxha) to arrange supervised visitation after stabilization.
6. Social work to assess housing stability and support systems in Bern.

OPERATIVE REPORT

Patient Name: Yonas Gebre-Medhin
Date of Birth: 14-03-1984
Sex: Male
MRN: 8890-2214
Date of Surgery: 25-05-2024
Surgeon: Dr. Elena Rossi
Assistants: Dr. Marcus Weber, RN Sarah Jenkins
Anesthesia: General Endotracheal Anesthesia
Anesthesiologist: Dr. Paul Schmidt

Pre-operative Diagnosis:
1. Blunt abdominal trauma
2. Suspected splenic injury
3. Hemorrhagic shock

Post-operative Diagnosis:
1. Grade III splenic laceration
2. Hemoperitoneum
3. Blunt abdominal trauma

Procedure Performed:
Exploratory Laparotomy with Splenectomy

Findings and Course of Operation:
The patient was brought to the operating room in a stable but tachycardic state. After induction of general anesthesia and placement of an endotracheal tube, the patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A midline vertical incision was made from the xiphoid process to the symphysis pubis.

Upon entry into the peritoneal cavity, approximately 800 mL of free hemoperitoneum was evacuated. Inspection of the abdominal organs revealed a significant laceration of the spleen involving the hilum and extending to the superior pole (Grade III injury). The liver, stomach, small bowel, and colon appeared grossly intact with no other injuries noted. The mesentery of the small bowel was inspected and found to be intact.

A splenectomy was performed. The short gastric vessels were ligated and divided. The splenic artery and vein were ligated at the hilum. The spleen was removed and sent to pathology. Hemostasis was achieved. The peritoneal cavity was irrigated with 3 liters of warm saline. No drain was placed as the hemostasis was secure and the patient was hemodynamically stable. The fascia was closed with 0 Vicryl, the subcutaneous tissue with 3-0 Vicryl, and the skin with 4-0 Monocryl and steri-strips.

The estimated blood loss was 1200 mL. The patient tolerated the procedure well. He was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) in stable condition.

Pre-operative instructions were followed. Post-operative orders include monitoring for signs of bleeding, transfusion as needed, and early ambulation.

Dr. Elena Rossi
Attending Surgeon

[doctor] Good morning, Marta. I see you are here for your follow-up regarding the breast mass we discussed last week.
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I am a bit nervous. The results from the biopsy are still pending, aren't they?
[resident] Actually, the pathology report came in this morning, so we can go over the findings together.
[patient_guest] Can we start then? My sister has been very worried since the surgery.
[doctor] Certainly. First, let us look at the macroscopic description of the specimen. It was a 2.4 cm mass removed from the upper outer quadrant of your right breast.
[resident] The specimen was fixed in formalin and processed routinely. The tumor was well-circumscribed but had some fibrous bands extending into the surrounding tissue.
[patient] Does that mean it was just a lump? Or is it something worse?
[doctor] The term "well-circumscribed" is often a good sign, but the fibrous bands suggest it may have been pushing into the tissue. Let us look at the microscopic findings.
[patient_guest] I do not understand the medical terms. Can you explain what you see under the microscope?
[resident] Under high magnification, we see clusters of epithelial cells surrounded by a dense collagenous stroma. The cells are relatively uniform.
[doctor] There is no significant nuclear atypia or mitotic activity, which is reassuring. However, there is a small area where the cells appear slightly more crowded.
[patient] Crowded? Does that mean cancer?
[doctor] Not necessarily. This pattern is consistent with a phyllodes tumor, specifically a benign one, given the low cellularity and lack of malignant features.
[patient_guest] A phyllodes tumor? I have heard that word before. Is it dangerous?
[resident] Most phyllodes tumors are benign, but they can recur if not completely removed. We need to check the surgical margins.
[doctor] The margins are clear, with a distance of 5 mm from the tumor edge to the inked cut surface. This is a good outcome.
[patient] So, I do not need more surgery?
[doctor] Based on these results, no further surgical intervention is required at this time. However, close surveillance is essential.
[patient_guest] How often will I need to come back for check-ups?
[resident] We recommend clinical examination and ultrasound every six months for the first two years.
[doctor] Yes, and you should report any new lumps or changes in the breast or axilla immediately.
[patient] I live in Zurich, but I have a friend in Geneva who is a nurse. She has advised me to keep a diary of any symptoms.
[doctor] That is excellent advice. Your friend, I assume, is a professional in the healthcare field?
[patient] Yes, her name is Sofia. She works at the HUG hospital. I trust her judgment.
[resident] It is good to have a support network. Are there any questions about the specific cellular details?
[patient] The report mentions "leaves-like architecture." What does that mean?
[doctor] It refers to the shape of the stromal projections that extend into the cystic spaces, resembling the veins of a leaf. It is a classic histological feature.
[patient_guest] It sounds very technical, but I am glad it seems benign.
[doctor] We must remain vigilant. Although this is benign, phyllodes tumors have a higher recurrence rate than fibroadenomas.
[resident] We will schedule your next appointment for a routine follow-up.
[patient] When is the next appointment?
[doctor] We have booked you for March 14, 2024, at 10:30 AM.
[patient] That works for me. I can take the train from Zurich easily.

[patient] Will I receive a copy of the report?
[doctor] Yes, it has been sent to your personal email address. Please check your spam folder if it does not arrive within 24 hours.
[patient] Thank you. I will look for it.
[doctor] Do you have any other questions today, Marta?
[patient] No, I think we are covered. Thank you for explaining it clearly.
[patient_guest] We appreciate your time and patience, Doctor.

[doctor] good morning . i am dr . keller , your surgeon . today we are going to discuss the plan for your upcoming surgery . do you have your interpreter with you today ?
[interpreter] yes , i am here . i will translate for you . good morning .
[patient] good morning . thank you for seeing me . i am a little nervous about the operation .
[doctor] it is normal to feel that way . we want to make sure you understand exactly what will happen . can you tell me your full name for the record ?
[patient] my name is ayşe demirtaş .
[doctor] thank you , ayşe . you have been referred for a hernia repair . can you describe the symptoms that brought you here ?
[patient] i have had a bulge in my right groin for several months . it gets worse when i stand up or cough .
[doctor] does it cause pain ?
[patient] it is mostly uncomfortable , but sometimes it hurts if i lift something heavy . last week , i could not push it back in easily .
[doctor] that sounds like an incarcerated hernia . we need to repair this to prevent complications like strangulation . do you have any other medical conditions ?
[interpreter] she says yes . she has high blood pressure and takes medication for it .
[patient] i take amlodipine every day . my doctor in the clinic said it was well-controlled .
[doctor] and any history of diabetes ?
[patient] no , i do not have diabetes . my blood sugar is normal .
[doctor] good . do you have any allergies to medications or latex ?
[patient] i am allergic to penicillin . it gives me a rash . no latex issues .
[doctor] noted . do you smoke or drink alcohol ?
[patient] i quit smoking ten years ago . i do not drink alcohol .
[doctor] what about your lifestyle ? do you exercise ?
[patient] i am very active . i go to the local swimming pool every tuesday and thursday . i have been a member of the aquafit verein in heidelberg for five years .
[doctor] that is excellent . swimming is great for cardiovascular health , though we will need to pause that for a few weeks after surgery . where do you live ?
[patient] i live in heidelberg . my address is 14 lindenstraße, 69115 .
[doctor] thank you . who is your primary care physician ?
[patient] it is dr . weber . he manages my blood pressure .
[doctor] we will send a copy of the operative report to dr . weber . are you related to anyone with a family history of heart disease ?
[patient] my sister has high cholesterol , but no major heart problems .
[doctor] do you have any history of cancer ?
[patient] no . i have had my regular screenings .
[doctor] how is your hearing and vision ?
[patient] i wear glasses , but my vision is good . my hearing is fine with my hearing aid .
[doctor] do you have any difficulty swallowing or breathing ?
[patient] no , i do not .
[doctor] have you had any previous surgeries ?
[patient] i had a hysterectomy twenty years ago . it was an open procedure .
[doctor] that is helpful to know . it means we may expect some scar tissue in the abdomen . do you have any questions about the anesthesia ?
[patient] will i be asleep ?
[doctor] you will have a general anesthetic . you will be asleep for the entire procedure and will not feel any pain .
[interpreter] she asks if she will remember anything .
[patient] will i remember anything ?
[doctor] no , you will not remember the surgery itself . you will wake up in the recovery room .
[patient] how long will the surgery take ?
[doctor] it usually takes about one to two hours . you will likely be able to go home the same day or stay one night for observation .
[patient] i would prefer to go home the same day if possible . i have a cat to feed .
[doctor] we will try to arrange that if you recover well . we will use a mesh to reinforce the wall . do you have any concerns about mesh implants ?
[patient] is it safe ?
[doctor] it is a very common and safe procedure . the mesh helps prevent the hernia from coming back .
[patient] i trust you , doctor . i just want to be back in the pool soon .
[doctor] you can usually resume light swimming after six weeks , once the area is fully healed . we will give you specific instructions .
[patient] that sounds good .
[doctor] do you have anyone to drive you home after the surgery ?
[patient] my daughter , elif , will pick me up .
[doctor] that is good . driving is not allowed for a few days after general anesthesia . do you have any other questions ?
[patient] no , i think i am ready .
[doctor] great . we will schedule the surgery for next tuesday . please make sure you fast after midnight the night before .
[patient] i will tell my daughter . thank you , dr . keller .

POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: RIGHT INDIRECT INGUINAL HERNIA
PROCEDURE: LAPAROSCOPIC RIGHT INGUINAL HERNIA REPAIR WITH MESH

FINDINGS:
The patient was brought to the operating room in stable condition. General anesthesia was induced and maintained without complication. The abdomen was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. Three ports were placed: an 11mm umbilical port for the camera, and two 5mm ports in the right lower quadrant.

Upon insufflation and visualization, a right indirect inguinal hernia was identified. The hernia sac was found to be located within the internal ring, consistent with an indirect hernia. There was no evidence of bowel obstruction or strangulation. The sac was reduced into the peritoneal cavity. The internal ring was widened slightly, and a 10cm x 10cm polypropylene mesh was introduced and positioned to cover the myopectineal orifice. The mesh was secured using four tacks at the anterior abdominal wall. No active bleeding was observed. Hemostasis was confirmed. The ports were removed, and the skin was closed with subcuticular sutures and steri-strips.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no intraoperative complications. Estimated blood loss was less than 50cc. Urine output was adequate. The patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) in stable condition.

RE: Post-Acute Care Plan for Right Hip Fracture

ASSESSMENT
Mr. Huber, an 87-year-old male, presented to our clinic following a fall at home resulting in a non-displaced right femoral neck fracture. The injury occurred on October 20, 2023. He was treated conservatively with pain management and strict bed rest for 48 hours prior to admission to our outpatient rehabilitation program. His daughter, Clara (age 42), is the primary caregiver and has been briefed on home safety modifications.

Mr. Huber has a history of hypertension and mild osteoporosis. Previous physiotherapy visits on March 15, 2023, and May 2, 2023, focused on general balance training and core stability, which showed positive response but did not prevent this acute incident. His current pain level is 4/10 on the VAS at rest, increasing to 6/10 with weight-bearing attempts. Range of motion in the right hip is limited by pain, with flexion at 60 degrees and abduction at 25 degrees.

INTERVENTION
Initial physiotherapy sessions focused on pain modulation using cryotherapy and gentle passive range of motion exercises. We introduced isometric strengthening for the gluteal muscles and quadriceps to maintain muscle tone without stressing the fracture site. Gait training has begun with a standard walker and partial weight-bearing status as per orthopedic guidelines.

We have also addressed his fear of falling, which is evident given his recent history. Cognitive engagement and confidence-building exercises are incorporated into every session. Clara has been instructed on proper transfer techniques and home environment adjustments, including the removal of loose rugs and the installation of grab bars in the bathroom.

PROGRESS
As of this report, Mr. Huber has attended 5 sessions over the past week. He demonstrates improved tolerance to active movement. Pain levels have decreased to 3/10 at rest. He is able to sit independently for 30 minutes and stand for 10 minutes with the walker. Balance in the semi-tandem stance has improved from 10 seconds to 25 seconds.

PLAN
We will continue with twice-weekly physiotherapy for the next 4 weeks. The focus will shift to strengthening and gait normalization. We anticipate transitioning to a single-point cane in 3 weeks, pending orthopedic review. Home exercise program has been provided digitally via email to a.huber87@mail.at.

Next scheduled follow-up with Dr. Weber: November 10, 2023.

Sincerely,

Mag. Anna Schiller
Physiotherapist, BSc

The patient is able to perform light domestic tasks such as cooking and cleaning. However, she has limited endurance for sustained physical activity. She cannot lift objects heavier than 5 kg. Prolonged standing is not tolerated due to the risk of syncope and worsening edema. She requires frequent rest breaks.

4. WORKPLACE IMPACT AND RESTRICTIONS
Given the patient's age (84) and the nature of her cardiac condition, she is NOT fit for heavy physical labor, machine operation, or any role requiring prolonged standing or climbing ladders.

If considering a sedentary, part-time advisory role, the following restrictions apply:
- Maximum working hours: 4 hours per day, 2 days per week.
- Must have a seated position with the ability to elevate legs.
- No requirement to stand for more than 10 minutes at a time.
- Immediate access to a restroom is required due to diuretic therapy.
- The workplace must be free of significant noise and stress triggers.

5. CONCLUSION
The patient is medically unfit for any role involving physical exertion, hazardous environments, or shift work. A sedentary, low-stress environment with frequent breaks is the only acceptable setting. Any deviation from these restrictions may lead to acute decompensation of heart failure.

We recommend a follow-up review in three months or sooner if symptoms worsen.

dialogue:
[pharmacist] good afternoon , ms . raman . i am anja , the hospital pharmacist . i see you have been admitted to the internal medicine ward for a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes .
[patient] yes , dr . kessler mentioned it this morning . it feels very sudden , to be honest . i have been feeling tired for months , but i didn't expect this .
[pharmacist] it is understandable to feel that way . the good news is that with the right management , you can live a very normal life . we are starting you on metformin 500mg .
[patient] metformin . i have heard that name before . my cousin has a friend who takes it . is it strong ?
[pharmacist] it is a first-line medication for type 2 diabetes . it works by helping your body use insulin more effectively and lowering the amount of glucose your liver produces .
[patient] i am a bit worried about side effects . i work long hours as a shift coordinator at the geneva cantonal hospital , so i need to be alert .
[pharmacist] that is a very important point . the most common side effect is some stomach upset , like nausea or loose stools , especially when you first start .
[patient] i see . i take care of my body quite a bit . i am a member of the swiss rowing club in lausanne , so i do not want to lose my stamina .
[pharmacist] metformin does not affect your physical performance or stamina directly . in fact , many athletes take it without issue . the key is to take it with food .
[patient] with food . so , with my breakfast and dinner ?
[pharmacist] yes , taking it with meals helps significantly to reduce the stomach upset . since you are starting at a lower dose , we are beginning with 500mg once daily .
[patient] once daily ? i usually prefer to manage my own health . can i just take it when i feel tired ?
[pharmacist] no , it must be taken at the same time every day to keep your blood sugar levels stable . intermittent use will not work effectively .
[patient] i understand . i am used to the strict schedules at the hospital . i will set an alarm on my phone for 8:00 pm .
[pharmacist] that is an excellent strategy . consistency is key . if you do experience any severe stomach pain or vomiting , you should stop and contact your medical team immediately .
[patient] what about my diet ? i eat a lot of rice and curries , as you might expect . will that interfere ?
[pharmacist] metformin does not interact with specific foods like rice or spices . however , managing your carbohydrate intake is crucial for diabetes control .
[patient] i see . i have been seeing dr . arjun vigneswara for my general health , but he referred me to dr . kessler here for the diabetes specialist care .
[pharmacist] that is a good referral . dr . vigneswara will be keeping in the loop with your general health , while the endocrinology team here manages the diabetes .
[patient] yes . i am scheduled to see dr . kessler again next week . do you have the date ?
[pharmacist] your next appointment is scheduled for october 14, 2024 , at 10:30 am in the endocrinology clinic , room 402 .
[patient] october 14 . i will write that down . i have a rowing practice that morning , but i can shift it to the afternoon .
[pharmacist] that is fine . please bring your blood glucose log to that appointment . we will give you a meter and test strips today .
[patient] a meter . i am not very tech-savvy . is it complicated ?
[pharmacist] it is very simple . you just prick your finger , apply the drop of blood to the strip , and the meter shows the number . we will demonstrate it before you leave .
[patient] okay . i have a family history of diabetes . my sister has it , and my mother had it too . i guess it runs in the family .
[pharmacist] family history is a major risk factor . that is likely why your levels were higher . but lifestyle changes , like your rowing , are protective .
[patient] i am glad i can keep rowing . it is my main way of decompressing from work at the hospital .
[pharmacist] definitely keep it up . exercise helps insulin sensitivity . just be careful not to overexert yourself if you feel dizzy , which can happen if your sugar drops .
[patient] dizzy . how do i know if my sugar is too low ?
[pharmacist] symptoms include shaking , sweating , feeling hungry , or confused . if that happens , eat 15 grams of fast-acting sugar , like glucose tablets or juice , and wait 15 minutes .
[patient] i will keep some glucose tablets in my rowing bag .
[pharmacist] that is a very smart idea . do you have any other medications or allergies ?
[patient] no allergies . i take a multivitamin , but i will ask if that is okay to continue .
[pharmacist] multivitamins are generally fine , but let's check for any iron content , as iron can reduce metformin absorption if taken at the exact same time .
[patient] i will check the label . i take it in the morning , so that should be fine .
[pharmacist] yes , separating them by a few hours is good . do you have any questions about the pill itself ?
[patient] it looks small . is it easy to swallow ?
[pharmacist] yes , it is a standard tablet . if you have trouble swallowing , you can crush it , but since you are starting at 500mg , you should be fine swallowing it whole .
[patient] i am a bit anxious about this new routine . i am used to controlling my environment at work .
[pharmacist] it is a lot to take in . remember , we are here to support you . if you have questions between now and your next visit , call the diabetes nurse line .
[patient] is that number on the discharge papers ?
[pharmacist] yes , it is on the first page , along with your emergency contact information .
[patient] thank you , anja . i feel a bit more prepared now .
[pharmacist] you are welcome , ms . raman . you are doing the right things by asking questions and planning ahead .
[patient] i will take my first dose with my dinner tonight .
[pharmacist] perfect . rest well . we will see you at your follow-up in two weeks .
[patient] thank you .
